items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1976-02-13
items.q: I'm, I really like to, like to feel as though I'm, I'm, I'm being influenced by, by him right now. ... I didn't know him personally. You didn't know him personally. I didn't get to hear him in person.

ctx.x: And most piano players, I take it around that time, let's say, set in 1915 or 1910 or whatever. You were born in 1910. We're band pianists.

They weren't so pianists. Band pianists, right. And you see, a lot of the good pianists that had kind of left around here by the time that I was coming up. Jelly Roll had been, Jelly Roll was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Tony Jackson was gone. You had many, many, I guess, were still around here. You had many local fellows, local pianists around town. Steve Lewis was around here, which was an excellent, excellent black pianist. Wonderful. And, well, like…
Did they, did the marching bands play Dixieland? Was that a term?

items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1960-07-14
items.q: I think, I think Jelly Roll did a lot of, a lot of standout work on the piano too.

ctx.x: Yeah, that's right. That's right. It was more or less, uh, if you got a good banjo player, and a good drummer, uh, all, all you'd have to do was just, just work right along with that piano, work right along with that, that, that, with that octave in the bass, or a single note, as I said before, and with a, a chord in the right hand, using mostly a tonic. Because, in those days, we didn't use any fancy chords. We didn't use any of those flatted fifths, and those progressive harmonies that they use in the day. We…
I wanted to ask you something about that trumpet player that was playing in front of you, Bill Gillan? Bill Gillan?
